paper_metadata.title: An optimal grain boundary engineering approach to improving the mechanical properties of FeCoCrNi high-entropy alloys at different temperatures

evidence.quote: The influence of grain boundary engineering (GBE) on the mechanical properties of FeCoCrNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) at different temperatures was systematically examined.

samples.material_state: base material (homogenized, cold rolled 50%, annealed 900 °C for 20 min)

evidence.quote: The FeCoCrNi HEA ingot was melted and cast in a vacuum induction furnace using mixture of pure Fe, Co, Cr and Ni ( ≥ 99.9 wt%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere.

samples.material_state: homogenized, cold rolled 50%, annealed at 950 °C for 3 h (Non-GBE)

evidence.section: 3.5. Tensile properties at room temperature and elevated temperature
evidence.quote: Instead of the BM sample without GBE treatment, the sample that underwent a homogenization annealing followed by 50 %-reduction cold rolling and annealing at 950 ◦C for 3 h was chosen as the Non-GBE sample for a comparison.

samples.material_state: GBE treated (5% cold rolling + 900 °C for 4 h annealing)

evidence.section: 3.4. Microstructures annealed for different times after 5 %-reduction cold rolling
evidence.quote: Therefore, for the FeCoCrNi HEA, 5 %-reduction cold rolling followed by annealing at 900 ◦C for 4 h is the optimal GBCD optimization process; the samples in this state are therefore defined as GBE samples.

other.charge: pure Fe, Co, Cr and Ni (≥99.9 wt%)

evidence.quote: The FeCoCrNi HEA ingot was melted and cast in a vacuum induction furnace using mixture of pure Fe, Co, Cr and Ni ( ≥ 99.9 wt%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere.
The ingot was hot forged at 1200 ◦C and then hot rolled at 1050 ◦C, achieving a total thickness reduction of 50 %.
The ingot was hot forged at 1200 ◦C and then hot rolled at 1050 ◦C, achieving a total thickness reduction of 50 %.
Subsequently, the FeCoCrNi sheet underwent homogenization at 1200 ◦C for 2 h in an argon atmosphere, followed by water quenching to eliminate segregation.
To achieve a uniform fine-grained structure, the homogenized material was then cold rolled to a total reduction of 50 % and annealed at 900 ◦C for 20 min, which was considered as base material (BM).

evidence.section: 3.5. Tensile properties at room temperature and elevated temperature
evidence.quote: Instead of the BM sample without GBE treatment, the sample that underwent a homogenization annealing followed by 50 %-reduction cold rolling and annealing at 950 ◦C for 3 h was chosen as the Non-GBE sample for a comparison.

evidence.section: 3.5. Tensile properties at room temperature and elevated temperature
evidence.quote: Instead of the BM sample without GBE treatment, the sample that underwent a homogenization annealing followed by 50 %-reduction cold rolling and annealing at 950 ◦C for 3 h was chosen as the Non-GBE sample for a comparison.
Based on the GBCD results across varying levels of cold rolling reduction, samples from the batch with a 5 % reduction were selected for further detailed study.

evidence.section: 3.4. Microstructures annealed for different times after 5 %-reduction cold rolling
evidence.quote: Therefore, for the FeCoCrNi HEA, 5 %-reduction cold rolling followed by annealing at 900 ◦C for 4 h is the optimal GBCD optimization process; the samples in this state are therefore defined as GBE samples.

evidence.quote: Fig. 1 a shows the XRD results of the BM sample, indicating that it has a single-phase FCC structure.

evidence.quote: The microstructure of the BM sample consists predominantly of equiaxed and randomly oriented grains, with an average grain size (including twins) of approximately 8.7 ± 0.1 μ m, as shown in Fig. 1 b.
